metadata.title: Brad Gerstner and Geoffrey Canada — Invest America and Raising the Floor

conclusion: Gerstner and Canada argue you raise the floor instead of attacking success. The Invest America Act, signed July 4, 2025, opens a capital account with $1,000 in the S&P 500 when a child gets a Social Security number. About 3.7 million babies a year, and about 10,000 births a day, each get an account. The law also opened accounts for every child under 18, about 70 million, because Michael and Susan Dell and other donors said they would fund the grandfathered cohort the government would not. The child owns a slice of Walmart, Berkshire, and Apple.
background: EP501, Nov 17, about 84 minutes. Patrick first heard the idea from Gerstner in 2020, pacing a kitchen in COVID, and thought the politics would kill it. Canada's seed accounts for a handful of kids, including a program of about 25, could not scale. Gerstner talked with Stan Druckenmiller and others and then took the idea to a national account. Claiming the account is the remaining work.
important_facts: The design. Two responses to the gap between billionaires and everyone else: attack success, or raise the floor. Gerstner picked the floor in 2020. Seed programs, including Canada's, proved the feeling of ownership and could not reach a national crisis. The Invest America Act was signed July 4, 2025. A child born in America gets a Social Security number and an account with $1,000 in the S&P 500. That birth class is about 3.7 million a year. Over 20 years of newborns alone you would reach about 60 million kids. They grandfathered everyone under 18 instead. The government would not fund that larger set. Private donors did. Gerstner went to Michael and Susan Dell and others. If you build it, they would fund it. About 70 million accounts now exist. In a few months each is supposed to hold money. About 10,000 children are born each day, and each of those accounts is opened with $1,000. Parents claim it in an app with a Social Security number. Rural Indiana, the South Bronx, and Compton get the same claim. The hard step is zero to one. One to two is easier. Family, employer, and philanthropic dollars can follow, including five and ten dollar contributions, on the model of a 401k.

What the child owns. The account is the S&P 500, so the examples Gerstner uses are a slice of Walmart, a slice of Berkshire Hathaway, and a slice of Apple, visible on a phone. That is the point of a universal capital account rather than a savings bond or a lecture. Canada has spent more than 50 years on poverty. He thinks it would be a mistake not to use this to create the next generation of capitalists, and that those capitalists will mostly be poor people. The old seed model made the child do something to receive the money. This one opens the account first. The parent still has to claim it. Gerstner separates created accounts, about 70 million, from claimed accounts. Patrick asks for the claimed percent and the answer on the tape stays on the created number: the original plan was only the 250th-birthday birth class, and the under-18 expansion is why donors, not the Treasury, fill the older accounts.

Why 2020 became a statute. Gerstner saw prosperity compounding for people who already owned capital and the opposite for people who did not. A pilot of 25 kids could not be the national answer. Druckenmiller and Canada were early conversations. The political difficulty Patrick assumed in 2020 did not stop the July 4, 2025 signing. The remaining operating problem is claiming: an account that exists and is unclaimed is not yet a household that knows it owns Walmart, Berkshire, and Apple. Employers and grandparents can add money once the account is real. Gerstner frames that as financial independence, not a transfer that replaces work. Canada frames it as the first time poor children start inside capitalism rather than next to it.

mental_model.name: Raise the Floor × $1,000 at Birth × Claim the Account
mental_model.components: Do not attack success. Open a capital account. July 4, 2025 makes $1,000 in the S&P 500 automatic with the Social Security number. About 3.7 million births a year and about 10,000 a day. Grandfathering the under-18 cohort creates about 70 million accounts. Treasury funds the newborns. Dell and other donors fund the older children. Claiming is the step from an account that exists to a household that knows it owns a slice of Walmart, Berkshire, and Apple. Zero to one is the hard part. A 25-kid seed could not do this.
mental_model.application: AAPL, BRK.B, and WMT are the three names Gerstner uses for what the child can see. The vehicle is the S&P 500, not a stock pick. The diligence is the claim rate, not the existence of 70 million empty logins. Do not treat the donor cohort and the Treasury cohort as the same funding.

key_insights.view: Raise the floor. Do not attack the people who already own capital.
key_insights.question: What is the account?
key_insights.answer: $1,000 in the S&P 500 when the Social Security number is issued. About 3.7 million newborns a year. About 10,000 accounts opened a day.

key_insights.view: Seventy million accounts exist. Claiming is the work.
key_insights.question: Who pays for the older kids?
key_insights.answer: The government would not fund every child under 18. Michael and Susan Dell and other donors said they would. Parents claim the account in an app.

key_insights.view: The child should be able to see a company they own.
key_insights.question: Which names does he use?
key_insights.answer: Walmart, Berkshire Hathaway, and Apple, on a phone. Canada thinks the next capitalists will mostly be poor kids if this is actually claimed.

top_investment_implications.thesis: One of the three companies Gerstner says a child can see they own through the S&P account — low
Named alongside Apple and Walmart as a slice of the birthright account, not a separate stock pitch — low
The third named holding a child is supposed to recognize on the phone — low
